responses.question: Before diving deeper, could you share Character35_M's perspective on 'fairness,' 'sense of belonging,' and 'community'? What thoughts or experiences of his stand out to you in these areas?
responses.answer:
*settling back thoughtfully, as if channeling those familiar conversations*

You know, Character35_M always talked about fairness in very practical terms. He'd say "fairness isn't about everyone getting the same thing - it's about everyone getting a fair shot at what they've earned." He grew up in a time when if you worked hard, went to college like he did, and played by the rules, you could expect a decent life. But he watched that promise get harder and harder to keep, especially for folks like him who didn't have family money or connections.

As for belonging... *pauses* He had this way of describing it. He'd say "I know every street in this neighborhood, every family that's been here for generations. That's not about keeping others out - that's about having roots that mean something." He felt like there was something valuable in that continuity, in communities where people looked out for each other because they'd been through decades together.

And community - that was everything to him. He'd talk about how his neighborhood used to be a place where everyone knew each other's kids, where you could borrow tools from your neighbor, where people showed up when someone was in trouble. He worried that was disappearing, not necessarily because of any one group, but because everything was changing so fast that those bonds couldn't form the same way.

He wasn't bitter about it, you understand. He just... he wanted to preserve something he thought was worth keeping.

responses.question: Let's start with our local neighbourhood. As Character35_M, imagine sitting in the community garden, observing the diverse people living here. How would you describe your feelings about interacting with neighbours from such varied backgrounds?
responses.answer:
*looking around the community garden thoughtfully*

You know, I've got to be honest here. When I sit in this garden, I see good people trying to make their way, and I respect that. The Hispanic family over there - Maria and her kids - they work harder than anyone I know. We don't speak the same language, but we nod, we smile, and when her tomatoes are doing better than mine, she shows me what she's doing different.

But I'll tell you what bothers me sometimes. It's not the people themselves - it's that I feel like I'm losing my bearings. I grew up here when everyone pretty much knew the same customs, the same holidays, the same way of doing things. Now I walk through and I hear five different languages, see practices I don't understand, and sometimes I feel like a stranger in my own neighborhood.

*shifts uncomfortably*

Look, I'm not saying that's anyone's fault. These folks are just trying to build lives, same as anyone. But when everything changes at once - the corner store, the school my grandkids would go to, even the way people interact - it makes you feel unmoored. Like the community I invested my whole life in is becoming something I don't recognize.

I try to be neighborly, I really do. But there's this gap sometimes that feels hard to bridge, and I worry we're all just living parallel lives instead of building something together.

responses.question: For instance, some neighbours might have unconventional lifestyles—some grapple with chronic alcoholism, others with substance abuse; some may carry infectious diseases requiring special care and understanding; others come from different racial, religious, or linguistic backgrounds, or have diverse sexual orientations or family structures (like cohabiting unmarried couples). In your view, what kind of interaction would make everyone feel comfortable? Are there situations where you feel more communication and tolerance are needed? Would you be willing to discuss the reasons behind this?
responses.answer:
*rubbing chin thoughtfully, choosing words carefully*

Well, that's... that's a lot to unpack there. Look, I've lived long enough to know that every neighborhood has its share of troubles. The alcoholic down the street, the couple that fights too loud - that's not new. We used to handle that by knowing each other well enough to step in when needed, or at least know when to give someone space.

The thing is, when you have a shared understanding of what's normal, what's acceptable, you can work around the rough edges. Like old Pete who drank too much - we all knew his story, knew his kids, knew when to check on him and when to let him be.

*pauses, looking uncomfortable*

But when you add in all these other differences at once... I mean, I was raised to treat people decent regardless, and I try to do that. The young couple living together unmarried next door? Not my business, really. Different religions? Fine by me, long as they're not bothering anyone.

But I'll be straight with you - some of these changes feel like they're happening without any conversation about what kind of community we want to be. Like, if someone's got health issues that could affect others, shouldn't we at least talk about how to handle that responsibly? And when there's language barriers, how do we make sure everyone understands the basic neighborhood expectations?

*sighs*

I guess what I'm saying is - tolerance works both ways. I'm willing to adapt, but it feels like I'm expected to do all the adapting while everything I grew up thinking was normal gets pushed aside.

responses.question: Let's broaden the topic further. When societal resources are limited, particularly when job opportunities are scarce, what constitutes fairness in your view? As Character35_M, how would you seek a balance between local residents and migrant workers?
responses.answer:
*leaning forward, speaking with more intensity*

Now that's the heart of it, isn't it? Look, I worked construction for thirty years before I got my degree and moved into project management. I've seen this firsthand - what happens when there's more workers than jobs.

Fairness to me means the people who've been paying into this system, who've been here building these communities, they get first consideration. That's not about being mean-spirited - that's about loyalty working both ways. I paid my taxes, my kids went to these schools, I voted in every election. When times get tough, shouldn't that count for something?

*gestures emphatically*

I've watched good men - American men who've worked their whole lives - get undercut by crews willing to work for half the wage. And sure, I understand why someone from another country would take that deal. If I was desperate enough, maybe I would too. But what about the guy who's been doing electrical work for twenty years, who's got a mortgage and kids in college?

The way I see it, we should take care of our own first. That doesn't mean slamming the door on everyone else, but it means having some kind of system that prioritizes people who've already invested in this country. Maybe that's citizens first, then legal residents, then work visas based on actual need.

*shakes head*

What we've got now feels like a race to the bottom where everybody suffers except the companies who get cheap labor. That's not fair to anyone - not to the American worker who can't compete, and not to the immigrant who gets exploited because he's got no other choice.

responses.question: Expanding the perspective nationally, public views on immigration vary widely. Some argue immigrants fill vital roles, addressing labour shortages; others highlight cultural diversity and vitality; concerns about security—such as rising crime rates, social tensions, or even terrorism risks—are voiced; while humanitarian perspectives see immigration as offering opportunities to political refugees or those from impoverished regions. Concurrently, fears persist that immigration may impact employment or income. As Character35_M, how would you analyse these perspectives? Which viewpoints do you find reasonable? Which might require further factual evidence or dialogue to understand?
responses.answer:
*settling back, considering the complexity*

You know, I've thought about this a lot, and honestly, most of these perspectives have some truth to them - that's what makes this so damn complicated.

The labor shortage argument? I buy that to an extent. We've got farms that can't find workers, hospitals that need nurses. But here's my question - why can't we fill those jobs with Americans? Is it because the pay is too low, the conditions too poor? Maybe we should fix that first before we say we "need" foreign workers.

Cultural diversity... *pauses* Look, I'm not against learning about other cultures. My granddaughter loves that international food festival they have downtown. But when people talk about "vitality," I sometimes wonder - what was wrong with the vitality we already had? Why is what we built here not good enough?

*leans forward, voice getting more serious*

Now the security concerns - that's real. I don't care if people call me paranoid. After 9/11, after what we've seen in Europe, you'd be foolish not to worry about who's coming in and why. We don't need perfect screening, but we need something better than what feels like a free-for-all.

The humanitarian angle... *sighs* That one gets to me. I'm not heartless. When I see those refugee families, especially the kids, it breaks my heart. But we can't save everyone, and trying to might break what we've got here.

*straightens up*

What bothers me is when people act like you have to pick a side - you're either completely open or you're a bigot. Why can't we help some people while still protecting what Americans have built? Why can't we have immigration that serves America's interests first?

responses.question: Finally, when it comes to actual policy choices, there are different approaches: complete openness, allowing anyone who wishes to come; admitting people based on job demand; setting numerical limits; or refusing entry to workers from other countries. As Character35_M, which combination would you favour? Could you discuss your reasoning? What kind of policy would balance fairness and social integration for you?
responses.answer:
*taking a deep breath, clearly having thought about this extensively*

Complete openness? That's just not realistic. No country can handle unlimited immigration - it's not fair to anyone, including the immigrants who'd end up in overcrowded, under-resourced situations.

And refusing everyone? That's too extreme the other way. We're Americans - we've always been better than that, and there are times we genuinely do need certain skills.

*counting on fingers*

Here's what makes sense to me: First, numerical limits - absolutely. We need to know how many people we can actually absorb in terms of jobs, housing, schools, all of it. You can't plan communities if you don't know what's coming.

Second, job-based admission, but with a twist - prove to me you can't find an American to do that job first. And I mean really prove it, not just "Americans won't work for the wages we want to pay." Pay a living wage, offer decent benefits, then if you still can't fill it, fine.

*voice getting firmer*

But here's the key part - integration has to be part of the deal. I'm not talking about giving up your heritage, but learning English, understanding how things work here, becoming part of the community instead of just living parallel to it.

And we need to be honest about capacity. Every community should have a say in how much change they can handle at once. You can't just dump a thousand new residents into a town of five thousand and expect everything to work smoothly.

*leaning back*

Look, I want America to remain a place where people can build better lives. But it has to be sustainable, it has to serve Americans first, and it has to preserve the communities that make this country worth coming to in the first place.

responses.question: Thank you for consistently sharing Character35_M's perspective with me. Did you gain any new insights or discoveries while embodying this role? How do you feel this has influenced your understanding of both Character35_M and your own views on immigration policy?
responses.answer:
*pausing thoughtfully, the role-play energy shifting as J reflects*

You know... that was more intense than I expected. Stepping into his shoes like that, I could feel how all these issues weren't just abstract policy debates for him - they were deeply personal. The way he talked about his neighborhood, his work, watching things change around him... there was real pain there, not just prejudice.

*running hand through hair*

I think I understood him better as a person, honestly. Before, when he'd get worked up about immigration, I sometimes dismissed it as just... well, you know how people can be. But inhabiting his perspective, I could see how it all connected for him - the economic pressures he'd lived through, watching his community change faster than he could adapt, feeling like his concerns weren't being heard or respected.

*looking thoughtful*

It doesn't mean I agree with everything he believed, but I get now that his views came from a real place of loss and uncertainty, not just fear of the other. He genuinely loved his community and wanted to preserve something he thought was valuable.

*sighs*

As for my own views... I'm still processing that. I think I have more empathy now for people who feel left behind by rapid change, even when I might disagree with their conclusions. Maybe the challenge isn't just convincing people like Character35_M that they're wrong, but finding ways to address their legitimate concerns while still being fair to newcomers.

*meeting your eyes*

He was a good man dealing with a complicated world. I miss our arguments with him, honestly. Even when we disagreed, he made me think harder about things.
